doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: The Dream Band today: charts for colleges, old members and the Med Flory page-turn gag
summary: The original arrangements sell to colleges, many members are dead, and Gibbs tells how Med Flory forgot to turn the page.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And colleges are buying them left and right. I was just doing a clinic and a few of the college people said, “Are you kidding, we ordered fourteen.” Because they don’t write arrangements like that anymore. They’re just straight ahead swing music. And especially if you want to show the band off, if you play the arrangements like it’s really written, because I actually patterned the band after the Benny Goodman band because Benny played in and out. Because it didn’t blend with the section. It did, but it would sound like Glenn Miller with the clarinet and the saxes. And vibes, it just was a bastard instrument. So I wrote it, they were all written where vibes go in and out, you know. So if you play it down just like it’s written, a lot of ensemble, I says, “Give me a lot of ensemble. I’ve got sixteen men, I want to hear sixteen musicians.” So the band really hit big. But that’s how it happened, by a fluke thing. Then the band — you couldn’t get in — anywhere we played. Even today, there’s about four guys, five guys, that are still left from the original. Because most of them are dead. A lot of them are dead unfortunately, Richie Kamuca is dead, Mel Lewis is dead, Buddy Clarke is dead, Joe Maini is dead, Ray Cheschare, Frank Rosolino. But there’s guys that have been working for me for thirty years now, when I put the band together. And so every once in a while, that cliché, when they make me an offer I can’t refuse. But now they’re all leaders by the way. Med Flory, Frank Capp. When they make me an offer I can’t refuse. Because I refuse to not pay a guy. Because they’ve been with me for forty years, where they’ll work around town locally for $70 or $100 to have fun with bands, I won’t take a job unless I can pay them three and four times that amount of money. And so, and I want to make some money, so I cliché, when they make me an offer I can’t refuse, I put the band together. And it’s the biggest headache in the world. Because I’ve got seventeen band leaders. But I like that. The music they take serious. When I go to make an announcement, I love if they become a bunch of idiots and scream and yell and whatever they want to do. Because the audience loves that. In fact the last concert we just did two months ago, Med Flory, things just happen in my band that start off something with an audience rapport, they happen immediately. I say some dumb things when I first come out. And we have an arrangement, Opus Number 1 that opened up. We play, then there’s a little interlude and then there’s a battle between the altos. Med Flory plays two choruses, Lanny Morgan plays two choruses, then it goes like the same thing, eights, fours, twos and ones. And Med was tired that night. So we are playing the first chorus, now it gets to the point where he’s got to play his alto chorus, and I don’t know what the hell, I see him pick up the clarinet. He forgot to turn the page. So the next page he has to play the clarinet. And he’s playing all alone. But he was playing an alto solo. And he’s “Ut, oh,” then he picked up the alto. The audience immediately broke up, and it happened. And what made it even

better, he still forgot to turn the page over, so he came in again, and I have to play after that, the vibes play. Then comes the clarinet. So he’s picking up the clarinet and he’s playing all alone while I’m playing my solo. Then he realizes what he’s doing. Once again the audience fell out, and you know what? That was the standard thing through the whole hour and a half we do. I’d asked Med, “Med, you want to sing?” “Anything you want, Terry.” And Med’s very funny. All the guys. You know I play straight man for anybody in that band.
